title: It Doesn’t Get Better Than This
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                John Galliano pulls out of a show at The Met, the eternal bond between Lee Krasner and Jackson
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                John Galliano pulls out of a show at The Met, the eternal bond between Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock, and Alex Katz keeps it moving at 99.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            Scrolling on Instagram, I stumble upon a clip of a 25-year-old guy from Chicago walking by the water after finishing work at his finance job. He tells us that he’s on his way to his downtown apartment, where his girlfriend and his new puppy are waiting for him, and that later he plans to go get beers and watch college football with his friends. “And I gotta say, I don't think life gets much better than this,” he concludes, brimming with positivity. “It's mid 70s, the sun is out … Is this peak? I think I'm peaking right now.”What a lovely reminder to be grateful for life’s little things, I think to myself. Inspired, I share the video with my wife, because I want her to peak, too. She replies, “LOL, is this real?”The biggest art story of the week is about John Galliano, a fashion designer who was convicted of antisemitic and anti-Asian hate speech in France in 2011, and has once confessed his love for Hitler. This week, he pulled out of an exhibition at The Met’s Costume Institute after public and donor outcry. Until three weeks ago, I had no idea who Galliano was. I guess I’m not a big Vogue reader. If I had a time machine, I’d zap myself back to the day before I found out. But you take the good with the bad. Next month, I’ll be rounding out my first year as editor-in-chief. I think you'll enjoy what we have planned for this fall. I’m blessed with an excellent team. Meanwhile, tensions between a hostile barista and me reach a boiling point when a glass bottle falls on the floor and shatters. She’s been giving me the stink eye for weeks while a poster behind her declares, “ICE Is Not Welcome Here.”Out on the street, I find myself feeling jealous of a concrete mixer truck. It's constantly processing what’s inside, never letting any of it harden. I watch an interview with 99-year-old American painter Alex Katz. “Get outside yourself and move,” he tells the reporter.  On my way home from work, I get hit with a sudden urge to make a detour onto Orient Avenue. A large park reveals itself and I go in for a stroll. I see people jogging or walking their dogs. Others are playing tennis, basketball, or squash. Skaters swing up and down in the air. One guy on a bench is halfway through Anna Karenina; two others are typing on their laptops, but by the looks of them, they must be completing manuscripts. The voices of merry children in the playground rise up to the sky. It's upper 70s; the sun is still out; and I gotta say, I don't think life gets much better than this.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief 

	
		
			What I Got Wrong About Krasner and Pollock
		
	
	
		Earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming exhibition Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous on Instagram, alongside a photograph of the artists by Hans Namuth. Seething, I looked to the comments for affirmation. I didn’t have to scroll for long. “Give her a solo show!”

Months earlier, I had visited the Pollock-Krasner House in Springs, East Hampton, knowing far more about Jackson Pollock than I did Lee Krasner. I am a painter myself, and I had come to Springs in the wreck of yet another failed relationship … with a painter. I thought I already knew Krasner’s story. I thought her story was partly my own. | Lia Strasser

Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.  The British Museum hosts Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel for a VIP viewing of the Bayeux tapestry, drawing concerns among staff.Following this week’s news of Yayoi Kusama’s passing, artists, galleries, museums, and fashion houses around the world take to social media to reflect on the seismic loss. Thieves make off with a platinum and diamond necklace from the Museum of Applied Arts in Vienna.Demolitions at the Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall in Tbilisi, Georgia prompt outcry from local community members and the architects.A new exhibition in NYC celebrates Snoopy’s enduring influence on art and fashion.Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich demands that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu order the dismantling of 40 Palestinian memorials in the Occupied West Bank.Art Movements: Mildred Howard wins the Artists’ Legacy Foundation Award, artists receive funding from the Anonymous Was A Woman Environmental Art Grants, Art Gallery of Ontario director steps down, Alex Katz on PBS, and more. A View From the Easel: printmaker and self-proclaimed “mountain ultrarunner” Hilary Lorenz transforms paper into boats, books, and weavings in the studio she built herself.In Memoriam: we honor Geles Cabrera, a sculptor who explored the body; Helch, a street artist who upset Queen Elizabeth; Jay Maisel, a commercial photographer who shaped the medium, and others. title: Vietnam Veterans File Restraining Order to Block Progress on Trump’s 250-Foot Triumphal Arch
description: A group of Vietnam veterans filed for a temporary restraining order on Friday to stop progress on one of Trump’s projects to alter the landscape of
body:
A group of Vietnam veterans filed for a temporary restraining order on Friday to stop progress on one of Trump’s projects to alter the landscape of the nation’s capital, a 250-foot triumphal arch. 

	The plaintiffs are veterans Michael Lemmon, Shaun Byrnes, and Jon Gundersen, along with architectural historian Calder Loth, who are represented by the Public Citizen Litigation Group, of Washington, D.C. They filed their motion for a 14-day restraining order on Friday, after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X on Thursday that “excavation work” for the arch would come within two weeks, promising that the arch would be “one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World.” 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The arch, however, has not received congressional approval. It is slated to go up at Memorial Circle, across the Potomac River, in Arlington, Virginia, from the Lincoln Memorial. The president debuted a model of the monument in October 2025, telling CBS News that the arch is dedicated to himself. Trump wants his arch, at 250 feet, to be taller than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, which rises to 162.5 feet. The plaintiffs argue that the arch would disrupt sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

	The veterans first filed suit in February against Trump; Vince Haley, of the president’s office; and the National Park Service (NPS), aiming to stop progress on the project, absent authorization from Congress. In April, they agreed to dismiss their motion in exchange for assurances that NPS would not authorize construction without posting a notice of its authorization online and that NPS would provide at least 14 days’ notice prior to beginning construction or demolition ahead of construction. 

	“The imminent course of action that Secretary Burgum has announced to the American people is unlawful many times over,” the Friday filing reads, further alleging that it violates the court’s April order. It adds that “once a building project has begun, a later order to reverse course raises ‘significant’ practical problems,” and that the defendants “have offered no evidence that beginning construction of a commemorative arch is a matter of such exigency that blocking construction until this Court has had the opportunity to rule on the project’s legality will irreparably harm Defendants or the public interest.”
	

	“This court,” conclude the plaintiffs, “should enter a temporary restraining order blocking Defendants’ efforts to blaze ahead with an unlawful course of conduct in the hope that they can render the arch a fait accompli before this Court has had the chance to reach a final determination as to whether Defendants’ project is authorized by law.”

	In a responding filing entered “to clarify Plaintiffs’ misunderstanding and avoid any potential for further confusion,” the Trump administration argues that the new activity will be “long-disclosed Phase 1B archaeological survey work,” conducted to ensure compliance with statutes such as the National Historic Preservation Act. “This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch,” it says, noting that the work will consist of digging four test pits. 

	The planning of the District of Columbia has been subject to great deliberation ever since it was founded in the late 18th century, notes the plaintiffs’ filing, with Congress responsible, since 1912, for authorizing any additional monuments and structures. 

	The Trump administration has shown no regard for Congressional or any other authority in his campaign to remodel the White House and Washington overall to suit his taste. This has included gilding large monuments near the Lincoln Memorial, adding Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center in violation of its founding documents, and abruptly removing a major Joel Shapiro work from the center’s grounds. 
	

	Most dramatically, he razed the East Wing of the White House without warning last October to make way for one of his favored projects, a massive ballroom-cum-military bunker that preservationists say would be out of proportion with the rest of the White House. Nonetheless, the Supreme Court ruled this week, 5–4, that construction could go ahead absent approval from Congress, saying that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to guard public buildings, which brought suit against the administration, did not have standing.

title: El Museo del Barrio and Aspen Conexión Look at the Rise of Latinx Art
description: This spring, El Museo del Barrio and Aspen Conexión hosted “The Rise of the U.S. Latino Art Market: Lessons from Latin America,” a half-day symposiu
body:
This spring, El Museo del Barrio and Aspen Conexión hosted “The Rise of the U.S. Latino Art Market: Lessons from Latin America,” a half-day symposium in El Museo’s iconic Teatro space.

	The event brought together artists, curators, museum directors, market insiders, and more to discuss the most pressing issues facing Latinx art in the art world and how to continue to grow its infrastructure. (ARTnews served as the media sponsor.)

	The idea for the event was dreamed up by Aspen Conexión, a division of the Aspen Institute focused on the Latinx community. Previously called Latinos & Society, it was founded, according to executive director Pilar Frank O’Leary, “around a simple but important idea that Latino impact in the United States is not only a domestic story but a hemispheric one across business, culture, finance, sports, and the arts. Latino communities are shaping markets, influencing global demand and redefine how we think about economic growth and cultural power across the Americas and beyond.”
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	In her introductory remarks, El Museo board chair Karla Harwich described the increased visibility that US Latinx artists are receiving as “a profound cultural shift” but “that there is still significant work to be done to ensure that this influence is matched by sustained institutional, equitable market investment, and long-term infrastructure.”

	“The questions we are exploring feel both urgent and long overdue,” Harwich said. “This is precisely why today matters.” 

	“We are gathering at a moment when Latino culture is increasingly redefining the American and the global mainstream,” Frank O’Leary added, calling it “the Bad Bunny era.”

	El Museo executive director Patrick Charpenel set the stage with one of the guiding questions for the day: “At El Museo del Barrio, we think deeply about how to translate cultural moments into structural change. What does it take to move from moments of visibility to lasting recognition?”

	One of the key points of the afternoon focused on how we could learn from the success of Latin American art both on the market and institutionally over the past two decades. “The rise of Latin American art over the past two decades did not happen by accident. It was built intentionally, through institutions, collectors, galleries, fairs, and sustained investment over time,” Aspen Conexión managing director Diego Deleersnyder said. Latinx art, on the other hand, is “still in an earlier chapter of that story.”
	

	A case study came in the form of a presentation titled “Building the Market: Latin American Art Fairs in Focus” by Diego Costa Peuser, the founder and global director of the Pinta Group, which stages numerous fairs and art weeks around Latin America and the US. Costa Peuser detailed the strategies that Pinta has taken, which includes a recent branch out to art weeks in different cities, like in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, and Panama City, to highlight the individual art scenes there. He concluded by saying, “In short, we understand that the growth of Latin American art does not occur spontaneously, but from sustained work.”   


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 convening “The Rise of the U.S. Latino Art Market: Lessons from Latin America,” at El Museo del Barrio.
									Courtesy Aspen Conexión
	



	The first panel, titled “Latin American and Latino Art in the U.S. Market: Galleries, Collectors, and Museums,” paired adviser Gabriela Palmieri, artist Emilio Perez, and Sotheby’s Latin American specialist Emily C. Nice, moderated by the Aspen Institute’s Danielle Baussan.

	Palmieri began by noting that even in the secondary market, Latin American artists are still rising. For example, she pointed to Leonora Carrington’s auction record being reset twice in two years: first at $3.3 million in 2022 and then a whopping $25.8 million in 2024. Institutionally, she pointed out how Wifredo Lam’s masterpiece The Jungle (1942—43) had long hung by the elevators at the Museum of Modern Art; last fall it received pride of place in the artist’s MoMA retrospective.
	

	Nice gave additional context about how Sotheby’s began holding Latin American art auctions after a specialist’s trip to Mexico in 1977. Both Carrington records were set at Sotheby’s, while Frida Kahlo’s El Sueño (La cama) reset the record for the most expensive Latin American artwork when it sold at the auction house for $54.7 million in November 2025.

	All of this is “something to get excited about,” Palmieri said, adding, “Context is key, placement is seminal, and excitement is real.”

	Perez, whose work is currently featured in “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way,” a survey of contemporary Latinx painting, said he wanted to join the day’s convening because he hasn’t always been included in conversations like this one. “Given my background, of course, I’m always going to be Latino—that’s who I see when I look in the mirror in the morning,” he said. “But when it comes to how the work is perceived, it really has so much to do with nuance. … As an artist, my interest [focuses on] being able to connect with a much broader audience, and sometimes I find labels to be somewhat of a constraint.”

	He added, “For any artist, the important thing is showing up every day, and when those opportunities happen, when those doors open, you have to walk through them.”
	


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 convening “The Rise of the U.S. Latino Art Market: Lessons from Latin America,” at El Museo del Barrio.
									Courtesy Aspen Conexión
	



	The day’s second panel, which I moderated, served as a rebuttal of sorts to the previous one. Titled “Decolonizing the Art System: Visibility and Invisibility in Latin American and Latino Art,” it included Silvia Cubiñá, executive director and chief curator of the Bass Museum of Art in Miami; Irene Gelfman, global curator for the Pinta Group; Patricia Hanna, director of the Jorge M. Pérez Collection and El Espacio 23; and Susanna V. Temkin, El Museo’s interim chief curator.

	“We talk a lot about the market, sales, record sales, and these works entering collections,” Hanna said, “but these works need to be seen, so how do people even know they exist if they don’t go to institutions and museums?” One approach is for El Espacio 23, founded by collectors Darlene and Jorge M. Pérez, to show the works in an annual exhibition, a must-see during Art Basel Miami Beach. “Our approach in terms of visibility is to really insert these artists into a more global conversation.”

	Another way, Temkin offered, is through exhibitions like El Museo’s La Trienal, which relaunched in 2021. Before joining El Museo, she worked as a Latin Americanist and assistant curator at the Americas Society. “It was only after being a part of exhibitions here that I realized what a platform El Museo in particular can be for the visibility of Latin American and Latino artists,” she said. “Shortly after the first Trienal, we witnessed [some featured artists’] work finally being acquired by major institutions.” (Hanna noted that the Pérez collection had acquired works from La Trienal.)
	

	While looking to Latin America can provide one path, Cubiñá cautioned against relying too much on that being the road map. “It’s a little bit of an unfair comparison,” she said, noting, first and foremost, the population size is tenfold: Latin America and the Caribbean at roughly 673 million while the US Latinx population at 68 million. She added that each country also has its own dedicated ecosystem of museums, galleries, and collectors. “Creating that [infrastructure]—which El Museo del Barrio does so well, and I think all of us try a little bit to—do is really important and the way forward.”

	The day’s keynote speech was delivered by E. Carmen Ramos, chief curatorial and conservation officer of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C. Drawing on her decades of experience as a curator, Ramos said, “I bring lived experience grounded in the belief that equal opportunity, curiosity, pride, and joy can help advance Latinx art in the present and future.”

	She then clarified that there is still much work to be done. “Our field, while undoubtedly better than in the not-too-distant past, still fails to fully recognize the realities facing many Latinx artists and institutions—their profound underrepresentation and their trailblazing leadership remain widely overlooked and underknown.”
	

	Ramos added that galleries, collectors, and critics are “essential partners” to curators and institutions like El Museo in these efforts. “I hope we leave today with a renewed sense of responsibility and possibility,” she said. “The stories we revisited, the artists we uplifted, the institutions we recognized—all reminders that progress is never incidental. It is built over the long haul through conviction, collaboration, and the courage to imagine something better.”

	Convenings like this one, Aspen Conexión’s Deleersnyder said in his closing remarks, show that “the talent is here, the cultural influence is undeniable, the demographic and economic momentum is significant,” and aim to help grow the infrastructure for Latinx art. “We hope today is not the end of a conversation, but the beginning of many more—across institutions, across markets, and across borders.”

schema.headline: El Museo del Barrio and Aspen Conexión Look at the Rise of Latinx Art

title: Kehinde Wiley Responds to the Trump Administration’s Removal of His Painting With an ‘Aesthetically Terrifying’ T-shirt
description: Kehinde Wiley’s artwork at the US Embassy in the Dominican Republic continues to cause a stir. Erin Scavino, director of Art in Embassies in a podca
body:
Kehinde Wiley’s artwork at the US Embassy in the Dominican Republic continues to cause a stir. Erin Scavino, director of Art in Embassies in a podcast interview with Sean Spicer, called the painting Young Artists After Siamesas 1960 (2013) “aesthetically terrifying” last week, but now in an unearthed radio interview from April, US ambassador Leah Campos described the painting as a lesbian picnic, according to the New York Times.

	In the interview conducted in Spanish, Campos said that she saw a “huge painting of a picnic in a park with flowers and some lesbians.” She wrongfully contends in the interview that the Biden administration wanted being “that ideology here to the Dominican people.” The painting was commissioned during the Obama administration by the State Department in 2013.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Wiley hasn’t come out publicly to address the controversy around his painting, but on his official e-commerce Instagram, he posted a black T-shirt retailing for $120 with the words “aesthetically terrifying,” which he borrowed from Scavino, who describes his work as such. “A response. A reclamation. A reminder that art has never needed permission to be beautiful, provocative, or powerful,” Wiley’s post reads.

	The Trump administration has been slowly changing artwork in its embassies to reflect “American patriotism and the beauty of our great country” as Campos put it in an Instagram post in August when describing the swap of Wiley’s painting for an image of the American flag accompanied by the Twisted Sister’s song We’re Not Gonna Take It.”

	At the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., the same act is taking place as workers began to disassemble Joel Shapiro’s monumental 24-foot-tall sculpture Blue. The American sculptor gave the center the work as a gift in 2019. The New York Times reported that Shapiro’s work was “targeted for elimination after President Trump’s takeover of the center.”

	In December, the center’s board, led by Trump and filled with his allies, voted to inscribe his name on the building’s facade, triggering an ongoing legal struggle with the federal court system.

title: Beyoncé Gives the Studio Museum in Harlem a $2 M. Gift on Her Birthday
description: Beyoncé Knowles turned 45 on September 4, and to mark the occasion, the global superstar entertainer made an unusual birthday gift, of $2 million, n
body:
Beyoncé Knowles turned 45 on September 4, and to mark the occasion, the global superstar entertainer made an unusual birthday gift, of $2 million, not to herself but to the Studio Museum in Harlem. 

	“Art tells all our stories; the past and the present, but is not always accessible to everyone,” said Beyoncé in a press release. “I have always been impressed with the Studio Museum in Harlem because of its intention to make the museum an integral part of the community. I have been introduced to several of my favorite young and upcoming Black artists through exhibits at the Museum. It is a place of inspiration where all audiences can discover new stories through the canvases of diverse storytellers that reflect our humanity.”
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The museum did not immediately respond to an email asking how the funds will be used; this story will be updated with any new information from the institution.

	Beyoncé is married to rapper, music mogul, and ARTnews Top 200 collector Jay-Z (born Shawn Carter). The couple famously shot large parts of the video for their 2018 single “Apeshit” at the Louvre Museum in Paris.

	“Each time Beyoncé releases new music, it might as well be considered an art-world event too,” wrote Alex Greenberger for ARTnews in 2020. “She’s been known to include works by vaunted artists in her videos, and with her husband Jay-Z, she’s built up an important collection of Black art.” He was writing on the occasion of the release of an 85-minute visual album titled Black Is King, which is “filled with artworks of note, and includes contributions from art-world figures behind the scenes.”

	One of the most-awarded performers of all time, Beyoncé has won 35 Grammy Awards, more than any other artist. As a solo musician, she has sold over 200 million records worldwide, and she is one of the highest-grossing live acts in history. Her net worth is estimated by Forbes to be $1 billion. 

	Founded in 1968 in a temporary space on the second floor of a Fifth Avenue loft building, the Studio Museum opened its new $160 million David Adjaye–designed home on 125th Street in November after a seven-year closure. Writing for ARTnews, Maximilíano Durón called it “stunning.” In 2023, the financier Joseph Perella and his wife Amy gave the museum a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting, making it one of the few US museums to own one. Also among the masterpieces on view at the reopening were works by Barkley K. Hendricks, Kerry James Marshall, Howardena Pindell, Faith Ringgold, and Carrie Mae Weems.
	

	“I am deeply grateful to Beyoncé, both for the generosity of this gift, especially on her birthday, and for recognizing the vital role that the Studio Museum plays in people’s lives,” said museum director and chief curator Thelma Golden. “Our institution was founded to shift the arts landscape and reimagine who that landscape serves. This gift will allow us to continue strengthening our work for Harlemites, New Yorkers, and audiences across the globe.”

schema.headline: Beyoncé Gives the Studio Museum in Harlem a $2 M. Gift on Her Birthday
